questions.q: How is the amine shown classified?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of an amine: a nitrogen atom bonded to an ethyl group, a methyl group and one hydrogen atom.

questions.solution: The nitrogen is bonded to two carbon atoms (an ethyl group and a methyl group) and one hydrogen, so this is a secondary amine, N-methylethanamine. Amines are classified by the number of carbons bonded to the nitrogen, not by the carbon the nitrogen is attached to.

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions convert bromoethane into ethylamine?

figure.alt: Bromoethane is converted into ethylamine; the reagents over the arrow are missing.

options.A: Aqueous sodium hydroxide, heated under reflux
options.B: Potassium cyanide in ethanol, heated under reflux
options.C: Excess ammonia in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube
options.D: Dilute aqueous ammonia at room temperature, with bromoethane in excess

questions.solution: Ammonia is a nucleophile that substitutes the bromine: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}Br + 2NH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2} + NH_{4}Br}\). It is used in excess, dissolved in ethanol, and heated in a sealed tube so the volatile ammonia does not escape. Aqueous hydroxide would give ethanol instead.

questions.q: When ethylamine is made from bromoethane and ammonia, why is the ammonia used in excess?

options.A: Ethylamine is itself a nucleophile, so excess ammonia makes it more likely that bromoethane reacts with ammonia rather than with ethylamine, reducing further substitution.
options.B: Excess ammonia acts as a catalyst for the substitution reaction.
options.C: Excess ammonia neutralises the ethylamine as it forms, so the equilibrium moves to the right.
options.D: Ammonia is a weak nucleophile, so it only reacts when it is concentrated.

questions.solution: The lone pair on the nitrogen of ethylamine can also attack bromoethane, giving diethylamine, triethylamine and finally a quaternary ammonium salt. With ammonia in large excess, a bromoethane molecule is far more likely to meet ammonia, so the primary amine is the main product.

questions.q: Propanenitrile, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CN}\), is reduced with lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) in dry ether. What is the organic product?
questions.solution: The C≡N group is reduced to \(\mathrm{CH_{2}NH_{2}}\), and its carbon stays in the chain: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CN + 4[H] \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\), propylamine. (A common slip is to forget that the nitrile carbon is counted in the name, giving ethylamine.) Hydrogen with a nickel catalyst does the same reduction.

questions.q: Which list puts ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine in order of base strength, strongest first?
questions.solution: The ethyl group pushes electron density onto the nitrogen, so its lone pair is more available to accept a proton than in ammonia. In phenylamine the lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available. So ethylamine > ammonia > phenylamine.

questions.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ammonia?

options.A: The benzene ring releases electrons onto the nitrogen, so its lone pair is held more tightly.
options.B: Phenylamine is not soluble in water, so it cannot form hydroxide ions.
options.C: The lone pair on the nitrogen overlaps with the delocalised π-system of the ring, so it is less available to accept a proton.
options.D: The nitrogen in phenylamine has no lone pair, because it is used in bonding to the ring.

questions.solution: Base strength depends on how available the nitrogen’s lone pair is to accept H+. In phenylamine the lone pair is in a p-orbital that overlaps with the ring’s π-electrons, so electron density is drawn into the ring and the lone pair is less available than in ammonia. The ring withdraws, not releases, this electron density.

questions.q: Which reagents convert nitrobenzene into phenylamine, as shown?

figure.alt: Nitrobenzene is converted into phenylamine; the reagents over the arrow are missing.

options.A: Tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, heated, then excess sodium hydroxide
options.B: Concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids, below 55 °C
options.C: Ammonia in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube
options.D: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux

questions.solution: Nitrobenzene is reduced by tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{5}NO_{2} + 6[H] \rightarrow C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2} + 2H_{2}O}\). In the acid the product is the phenylammonium ion, so sodium hydroxide is added to release the free amine. Nitric and sulfuric acids make nitrobenzene; they do not reduce it.

questions.q: Butylamine reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. What is the product?
questions.solution: An amine is a base: the lone pair on the nitrogen accepts a proton from the acid. \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2} + HCl \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{3}^{+}Cl^{-}}\), a salt, butylammonium chloride. No substitution takes place.

questions.q: Ethanoyl chloride, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl}\), is added to an excess of methylamine. What is the main organic product?
questions.solution: The lone pair on the nitrogen of methylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon and HCl is eliminated: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + 2CH_{3}NH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONHCH_{3} + CH_{3}NH_{3}^{+}Cl^{-}}\). The product is a secondary amide, N-methylethanamide. Ethanamide would form with ammonia; an ester would need an alcohol.

questions.q: What type of mechanism takes place when ethylamine reacts with ethanoyl chloride, shown?

figure.alt: Ethylamine reacts with ethanoyl chloride to give N-ethylethanamide and hydrogen chloride.

questions.solution: The nitrogen’s lone pair attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon (nucleophilic addition, the C=O π-bond breaking). The C=O then reforms and a chloride ion is eliminated, and H+ is lost from the nitrogen. Overall this is nucleophilic addition–elimination; it is not a one-step substitution, because the carbonyl carbon is attacked first.

questions.q: Quaternary ammonium salts with long alkyl chains are used as cationic surfactants. In which product are they commonly found?
questions.solution: The positively charged head of the quaternary ammonium ion sticks to negatively charged surfaces such as wet fibres and hair, while the long hydrocarbon tail stays on the outside, reducing static and making the surface feel smooth. So they are used in fabric softeners and hair conditioners. Dyes are made from aromatic amines.

questions.q: Ammonia is heated with a large excess of bromomethane. What is the final organic product?
questions.solution: With bromomethane in excess, each amine formed is itself a nucleophile and is substituted again: methylamine, then dimethylamine, then trimethylamine, then \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{4}N^{+}Br^{-}}\). The quaternary ammonium ion has no lone pair, so substitution stops there. (Methylamine is the main product only when ammonia is in excess.)

questions.q: Butylamine is added a little at a time, and then in excess, to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. What is seen?

options.A: A pale blue precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution.
options.B: A pale blue precipitate forms, which does not dissolve in excess.
options.C: A green solution forms, which turns yellow in excess.
options.D: No change, because amines do not react with metal ions.

questions.solution: Butylamine in water is alkaline, so it first precipitates pale blue copper(II) hydroxide, \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{4}(OH)_{2}]}\). In excess, butylamine molecules act as ligands, as ammonia does, using the lone pair on the nitrogen, giving a deep blue solution of a complex ion.

questions.q: Which of these compounds is an amide?
questions.solution: An amide has a nitrogen bonded directly to a C=O carbon, the group \(\mathrm{-CONH_{2}}\) (or \(\mathrm{-CONH-}\)). Ethanamide, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CONH_{2}}\), is an amide. The first two are amines, and \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}COOH}\) is an amino acid: its \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\) is not on the carbonyl carbon.

questions.q: Which pair of reagents would react to make the amide shown, N-ethylpropanamide?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of the target amide: a C=O carbon bonded to an ethyl group on one side and to an N–H, whose nitrogen carries an ethyl group, on the other.

questions.solution: Split the amide at the C–N bond. The C=O side has three carbons, from propanoyl chloride, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}COCl}\); the nitrogen carries an ethyl group, from ethylamine: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}COCl + CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CONHCH_{2}CH_{3} + HCl}\). (Swapping the two groups gives N-propylethanamide, an isomer.)

questions.q: Why can amines act as bases?

options.A: They release hydroxide ions when they dissolve, because they contain OH groups.
options.B: They have a hydrogen atom on the nitrogen that can be donated as H+.
options.D: The nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons that can accept a proton.

questions.solution: A base is a proton acceptor. The lone pair on the nitrogen forms a dative bond to an \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ion: \(\mathrm{RNH_{2} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons RNH_{3}^{+} + OH^{-}}\). Amines contain no OH group; hydroxide ions form because water loses the proton.

questions.q: Ethylamine reacts with ethanoic anhydride. What are the products?
questions.solution: An acid anhydride reacts like an acyl chloride but eliminates a carboxylic acid instead of HCl: \(\mathrm{(CH_{3}CO)_{2}O + CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONHCH_{2}CH_{3} + CH_{3}COOH}\). (Hydrogen chloride forms only with an acyl chloride.)
